h1: Tasting beer at a corporate training session
title: Beer Tasting for Corporate Training | Craft Beer School
desc: How to run a responsible beer tasting inside a corporate training day: opt-in rules, pours, order, a one page sheet and how it ties back to the desk.
teaser: A good tasting turns a dashboard line like 'bitterness' into something your team has actually tasted. A bad one is a party with a lanyard.
standfirst: A guided tasting is the fastest way to make a beer, whisky or wine team understand the product behind the numbers. It only works when it is opt-in, small and tightly run. Here is the format we use and the rules around it.
sections: Why taste at all in a training session

Planners, buyers, analysts and finance teams in drinks companies often work with the product for years without tasting it in a structured way. A forecast for a wheat beer, a lager and a stout gets built from the same template. Then someone notices that the stout sells at a different time of year, in a different serve, to a different drinker. A 45 minute tasting explains a lot of that on its own.

The aim is not to make anyone a judge. It is to give everyone a shared vocabulary for what is in the glass, so the conversation about volume, price and range starts from something real.
Start with the rules, not the beer

Alcohol at work needs care. Before you plan anything, check the company policy and the rules for the venue. In India, whether alcohol can be served at an office or at an offsite depends on company policy and on state excise rules for the premises. Both change. When in doubt, hold the session at a licensed venue such as a brewery taproom and let the venue's licence do its job. This is process guidance, not legal advice.

Then set the ground rules on the invite:

  • Taking part is optional. Anyone who does not drink, or prefers not to, is welcome and has a full role.
  • Pours are small, about 30 ml. Spit cups and water are on every table.
  • Nobody drives afterwards. Book transport or hold the session early in the day.
Choose four beers that show different things

Four samples is plenty. Choose them to show contrast, not quality ranking:

  1. A pale lager: light body, clean finish, low bitterness.
  2. A wheat beer: cloudy, soft, often with banana or clove notes from the yeast.
  3. An India pale ale: high hop aroma and firm bitterness.
  4. A stout or porter: roasted malt, coffee or chocolate notes, fuller body.

Serve from light to heavy. Cold temperature hides flavour, so lager at about 4 to 6 °C is fine but ales are better at 8 to 10 °C. Use clean glasses and rinse with water between beers.
Teach four words once, then use them

Give the team four tasting terms and no more. Aroma is what you smell. Bitterness is the dry grip that lingers in the finish, driven by hops. Body is the weight in the mouth. Carbonation is the fizz. One label term helps too: alcohol by volume, or ABV, is the strength of the beer as a percentage.

A one page sheet helps. List the four terms down the side and the four beers across the top. People mark low, medium or high. Compare answers as a group. Different noses will disagree. That is the lesson: perception varies widely, which is why trained panels exist. Our guide to setting up a beer tasting goes deeper on the kit.
The floor detail: what the glass tells a planner

Take the stout. It is heavier, slower to drink and often bought in smaller volumes. A planner who has tasted it understands why a tank of stout can sit while the lager sells through. A buyer who has tasted a hazy IPA understands why it needs to be fresh. Hop aroma fades, so an old pack tastes flat. That explains why shelf life and cold chain show up as hard limits in a stock plan.

Connect each beer to one number your team works with: sell-through, shelf life, margin per litre or distribution reach. Do that out loud during the session.
Close the loop at the desk

Finish with ten minutes of discussion. Ask each table one question: which beer would you keep and which would you drop if you could only list three? Then ask what would change that answer. Often it is price or season rather than taste.

Follow up within a week with the one page sheet and a short note linking each beer to a business question. Our guide to running responsible tastings at work covers the policy side in more detail.
When a one-off tasting is not enough

One session gets people curious. It does not build a shared standard. Teams that need that, for example sales, planning and quality functions that argue about what 'good' means, need a repeated format with the same beers and the same sheet. We build those around the team's own portfolio and run them as guided sensory sessions inside a wider programme.
faqs: Can we hold a beer tasting at the office?
That depends on your company policy and on state rules for the premises, which change. A licensed venue such as a brewery taproom is often easier. Check the current rules or ask your legal team.
How much beer is a tasting pour?
About 30 ml per sample, with four to six samples at most. Provide water, spit cups and food. Nobody is expected to finish a glass.
What if some people do not drink?
They take part in the smelling, describing and discussion. Smelling needs no sip, so non-drinkers can describe every sample. Make sure they have a full role.
